Specify the thickness. IPC-CC-830 recommends 25-75 microns for most coatings, 12.5-25 microns for parylene. Too thin provides inadequate protection. Too thick increases stress on components during thermal cycling, can bridge between closely spaced leads causing shorts, and wastes material.

Define the cure process. UV-curable coatings: cure in seconds under UV lamp, shadow areas need secondary moisture cure. Thermal cure: 10-60 minutes at 60-80C for most coatings. Room temperature cure: 24 hours for acrylics (ties up production space). Moisture cure: for some silicones and polyurethanes, takes 24-72 hours depending on humidity.

steps.description: Specify the coating application process, masking procedure, cure profile, and inspection methodology to produce repeatable coating coverage in production.

inputs.name: selected-coating
inputs.desc: Coating product, application method, and thickness

outputs.name: coating-process-document
outputs.desc: Step-by-step process specification: surface preparation, masking, application, cure, de-mask, and inspection with acceptance criteria

outputs.name: rework-procedure
outputs.desc: Procedure for removing coating from specific areas for repair and recoating after component replacement

process: Specify surface preparation. The PCB must be clean and dry before coating. Residual flux, fingerprints, or moisture trapped under the coating cause adhesion failure and corrosion. Clean per IPC-A-610 requirements: deflux (if using no-clean flux, verify compatibility with coating), clean with appropriate solvent, and bake at 65C for 2-4 hours to drive off moisture.

Define the masking procedure. Masking options: peelable latex mask (hand-applied dots for test points and connectors), polyimide tape (Kapton) for straight-edge keep-outs, custom rubber boots for tall connectors. For selective spray: program the spray path to avoid keep-outs, but use masking as a backup for critical areas where overspray would cause functional failure.

Specify the application parameters. For spray: nozzle-to-board distance (150-200mm typical), spray pressure, fan pattern width, pass speed, and number of passes for target thickness. For dip: immersion speed (25-50mm/s), dwell time (3-5 seconds), withdrawal speed (sets the film thickness: slower = thicker). Record these parameters for process control.

Specify the inspection method. Visual inspection under UV light (most coatings fluoresce under 365nm UV): check for complete coverage in coated areas and absence of coating in keep-outs. Accept the coating if: no bubbles larger than 3mm diameter, no uncoated areas in the required zone (except component tops that are not specified for coverage), no bridging between closely spaced leads, and coating in keep-outs within the rework tolerance.

Write the rework procedure. For acrylic: apply solvent (butyl acetate or proprietary stripper) to the repair area with a brush, wait for the coating to soften, and peel or wipe away. Replace the component. Clean the area. Recoat using a brush, applying two thin coats with a 10-minute flash between coats. Re-inspect under UV. For silicone: carefully cut and peel the coating from the repair area using a scalpel, taking care not to damage adjacent components or traces.

description: Apply reliability-centered maintenance analysis to electronic and electromechanical systems to determine the optimal maintenance strategy for each failure mode, replacing calendar-based maintenance with condition-based decisions backed by failure data.

steps.description: Decompose the system into maintainable items and identify the functions each must perform, establishing the functional context for failure analysis.

inputs.name: system-description
inputs.desc: System architecture, operating context, and performance requirements

inputs.name: maintenance-history
inputs.desc: Available failure records, repair logs, and current maintenance schedule

outputs.name: functional-breakdown
outputs.desc: Hierarchical list of system functions at the system, subsystem, and component level, with performance standards for each function

outputs.name: maintenance-significant-items
outputs.desc: Items selected for RCM analysis based on safety, operational, or economic significance of their failure

process: Define the system's primary and secondary functions. A power supply's primary function: convert 120VAC to 12VDC at 50A with less than 1% voltage regulation. Secondary functions: provide short-circuit protection, provide input-to-output isolation of 4kV, operate without audible noise above 35 dBA.

Decompose to the lowest replaceable unit. For electronics: individual PCB assemblies, power supplies, fan assemblies, filter assemblies, batteries. Do not go below the field-replaceable level unless repair at a lower level is economically justified.

For each item, list all functions with quantified performance standards. A function without a performance standard cannot be analyzed for failure. 'Supply power' is not a function. 'Supply 12V +/-0.12V at 0-50A with less than 100mV ripple' is a function.

Screen items for maintenance significance. An item is maintenance-significant if its failure has safety consequences, if its failure stops production or mission, or if its failure costs more than preventive maintenance. Items with none of these consequences can run to failure.

Prioritize items by consequence severity. Safety-significant items must be analyzed first and most thoroughly. Operational items (production stops) second. Economic items third. This ranking drives the depth of analysis and the rigor of the maintenance task.

steps.description: Identify how each maintenance-significant item can fail, what causes each failure, and what happens when it does, using field data where available and engineering analysis where not.

outputs.name: failure-mode-catalog
outputs.desc: For each significant item: failure modes, failure causes, local effects, system effects, and failure evidence (how the operator detects the failure)

outputs.name: failure-distribution-data
outputs.desc: Available failure rate or time-to-failure distribution data for each failure mode from field data, vendor data, or handbooks

process: For each function, ask: how can this function be lost? How can it degrade? A power supply function 'supply 12V' can fail by: output goes to zero (total loss), output drifts high (degradation, overvoltage), output drifts low (degradation, undervoltage), output ripple exceeds limit (degradation). Each is a distinct failure mode requiring a different maintenance approach.

Identify failure causes for each mode. Output goes to zero: main switching MOSFET short circuit, control IC failure, input fuse opens due to capacitor degradation, solder joint fracture on power path. Each cause has a different failure pattern (random, wear-out, early-life) that determines whether preventive maintenance is effective.

Document the effects at three levels: local (what happens at the component), system (what the operator experiences), and safety (any hazard). A capacitor failure in a power supply filter: local = increased ripple, system = downstream circuits malfunction, safety = none for this example. If the effect were fire risk, the consequence classification changes dramatically.

Gather failure data. Best source: field failure records from the same or similar equipment. Second: manufacturer reliability data (MTBF, FIT rates). Third: handbook data (MIL-HDBK-217F, SN 29500, FIDES). Handbook data gives failure rates; field data gives failure distributions (Weibull shape and scale parameters), which are more useful for maintenance planning.

Classify each failure mode by its age-reliability pattern. The classic bathtub curve applies only to some failure modes. Electronic components typically show pattern E (constant failure rate) or pattern F (infant mortality decreasing to constant). Mechanical wear items show pattern B (wear-out). This classification determines which maintenance strategies apply.

steps.description: Apply the RCM decision logic to each failure mode to select the maintenance task that manages the failure consequence at the lowest total cost.

inputs.name: failure-mode-catalog
inputs.desc: Failure modes with effects and consequences

outputs.name: maintenance-task-assignments
outputs.desc: For each failure mode: the selected maintenance task (condition monitoring, scheduled restoration, scheduled discard, failure finding, run to failure, or redesign) with the task interval and justification

outputs.name: maintenance-schedule
outputs.desc: Consolidated maintenance schedule showing all tasks organized by interval (daily, weekly, monthly, annually, at overhaul)

process: Apply the RCM decision logic tree to each failure mode. First question: is the failure evident to the operator during normal duties? If no, it is a hidden failure and requires a failure-finding task regardless of consequence. Hidden failures in safety systems (backup power, redundant channels) are the highest priority for scheduled checks.

For evident failures, select the task based on consequence and failure pattern:
- Condition-based maintenance (CBM): monitor a parameter that indicates deterioration before functional failure. Effective for wear-out patterns (Weibull beta > 1). Examples: capacitor ESR measurement detects aging before failure, thermal imaging detects hot spots from degraded connections, vibration monitoring detects bearing wear. The P-F interval (time between detectable degradation and functional failure) must be long enough for corrective action.
- Scheduled restoration: restore the item to original condition at a fixed interval. Effective only if the failure mode has a well-defined wear-out age. Rebuilding a fan motor every 5 years is effective if bearings consistently wear out between 6-8 years. Not effective for electronic components with constant failure rates.
- Scheduled discard: replace the item at a fixed interval regardless of condition. The interval must be at the beginning of the wear-out region (Weibull beta > 1, interval set where the reliability curve begins to decline). Effective for items with low replacement cost relative to failure consequence.
- Run to failure: no preventive action; repair when it fails. Default for failures with low consequence and no detectable degradation pattern.

Calculate failure-finding task intervals for hidden failures. The interval must produce the required availability of the hidden function. If the safety system must be available 99% of the time: T_interval = 2 * (1 - A_required) * MTBF. For MTBF = 50,000 hours and 99% availability: T = 2 * 0.01 * 50000 = 1000 hours (approximately 42 days).

For failure modes where no maintenance task is both applicable and effective, and the consequence is safety-related, the answer is mandatory redesign. Redesign the system to eliminate the failure mode or make it evident. This is the only RCM answer that requires hardware changes rather than maintenance changes.

Consolidate all task assignments into a maintenance schedule. Group tasks by interval for efficient execution: combine all weekly checks into one procedure, all monthly checks into another. Align intervals with operational windows (maintenance during planned downtime). Calculate the annual maintenance cost and compare to the current maintenance program cost and the cost of unplanned failures.

steps.description: Implement the RCM-derived maintenance program and establish the feedback loop that updates maintenance tasks as field data accumulates, preventing the program from becoming static and obsolete.

inputs.name: maintenance-task-assignments
inputs.desc: Selected tasks for each failure mode

outputs.name: maintenance-procedures
outputs.desc: Work instructions for each maintenance task including what to inspect, how to measure, acceptance criteria, and actions if criteria are not met

outputs.name: feedback-mechanism
outputs.desc: Data collection requirements and review trigger criteria that update maintenance intervals as field experience grows

process: Write maintenance procedures that technicians can follow without RCM expertise. Each procedure must state: what to do (specific measurements or inspections), how to do it (tools, instrument settings, access procedure), what constitutes a pass (quantified acceptance criteria, not 'appears satisfactory'), and what to do if it fails (repair, replace, schedule corrective action, or declare the unit unserviceable).

For condition-based tasks, define the measurement technology and trending methodology. Example: electrolytic capacitor ESR monitoring. Measure ESR with an LCR meter at 100 kHz on each scheduled maintenance. Plot the trend. Set alert threshold at 2x initial ESR. Set action threshold at 3x initial ESR. The slope of the trend predicts remaining life.

Establish the age exploration process. For every failure mode currently assigned to run-to-failure or condition-based monitoring, track the failure age (operating hours or calendar time at failure). After accumulating 5-10 failure data points, fit a Weibull distribution. If the shape parameter beta exceeds 1.5, the failure mode is wear-out and may benefit from scheduled replacement at the characteristic life (63% of the population has failed).

Define the review triggers that prompt a maintenance program update: a failure that the maintenance program should have prevented, three or more failures of the same mode within a review period, new information from the manufacturer (service bulletin, reliability update), or a change in operating context (increased duty cycle, new environment).

Calculate maintenance effectiveness metrics after 12 months of operation. Track: unplanned failure rate (should decrease), maintenance cost per operating hour (should decrease or remain stable), system availability (should increase). If unplanned failures are not decreasing, the maintenance tasks are not addressing the dominant failure modes and the RCM analysis needs revision.
